item.title: Deadly disease outbreak kills 2,000 as experts reveal what Americans should know
item.description: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed over 2,000 people, but experts say the average American faces very little threat.
item.content:encoded:
As the death toll from the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) surpasses 2,000 people, infectious disease experts say Americans should remain aware of the humanitarian crisis overseas while understanding the reality of domestic risk.

The virus has spread rapidly across parts of eastern and northeastern DRC, with earlier cross-border cases in Uganda. Published government data shows a total of 4,381 confirmed cases.

"There's a lot of people who live there. So this is not breaking out in a town of 50, but in rural cities of hundreds of thousands," David Wohl, MD, a professor of medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told Fox News Digital.

FAUCI TEXTS SUGGEST OFFICIALS WERE ‘TOO SLOW TO PIVOT' AMID PANDEMIC, SAYS DR MARC SIEGEL

"Compared to previous outbreaks, the pace at which this is moving is unprecedented," he went on. "The slope is just so catastrophic, with more and more people getting infected at a very significant pace without much slowing down."

Controlling transmission has proven particularly difficult in the DRC due to what Wohl calls a "perfect storm" of adverse conditions.

MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

Dense populations and limited access can complicate efforts to deliver medical care, track contacts and establish quarantine protocols, he noted.

"There's conflict in and around these areas, which makes getting in and out of them … really tough," Wohl said.

Despite the escalating death toll in Africa, health officials emphasize that the average American faces very little threat from Ebola.

"This is not something that I think the average person has to worry about acquiring here in the United States," Wohl said, noting that transmission requires close physical contact with bodily fluids from a severely ill or deceased individual.

"It doesn’t travel across the air and across a room," he added.

Even during the massive 2014 West Africa outbreak, which Wohl said infected more than 28,000 people, only four Ebola cases were diagnosed in the U.S. Two were imported cases, and two nurses contracted the virus while caring for an infected patient in Dallas, according to the CDC. 

Several other Ebola patients who had been infected and diagnosed overseas were medically evacuated to the U.S. for treatment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We just have so much better public health, healthcare systems, hygiene, access," Wohl said. "It's a very different environment."

Viruses like measles, influenza, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 pose more immediate public health concerns for Americans, he added.

"The average person who gets a headache or a fever does not need to worry about Ebola," the doctor said.

For the U.S., potential concerns include the risk to healthcare providers traveling to Africa to assist with containment efforts and the possibility of further instability in the region.

Medical researchers are also navigating challenges with virus variants, according to Wohl.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

While treatments and vaccines were successfully deployed against the Zaire strain during the 2014 crisis, the doctor said the Bundibugyo virus circulating in parts of the DRC is genetically different. 

As a result, approved Ebola therapeutics are not approved for Bundibugyo-related disease, and their effectiveness against it has not been established.

Researchers are actively evaluating new treatments and vaccine candidates for Bundibugyo virus, Wohl said. 

Emerging technologies, including mRNA platforms, could potentially help researchers more rapidly develop vaccines against specific viral threats, according to the doctor.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Global agencies, including the World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, continue to monitor the region closely. Wohl emphasized that international support and resource deployment remain critical to stopping the surge.

"This is a fire that’s raging that continues to be out of control," Wohl said. "There’s lots of people suffering ... and I think more can be done."

item.title: AMBASSADOR GEORGE DEEK: The Christian Israel you are not being shown
item.description: Israel's envoy to the Christian world, raised Greek Orthodox in Jaffa, says Christians grew from 34,000 in 1950 to 184,000 and continue to flourish.
item.content:encoded:
I grew up in Jaffa, going to church every Sunday with my father, the cantor of our Greek Orthodox church. I joined the Christian Scouts as a boy, later became a leader in the movement and even ran our marching band, a serious source of community pride. We marched at Christmas and Easter. We celebrated weddings, baptisms and feast days. We knew which grandmother made the best food and which family was feuding with which other family.

In other words, we were a perfectly normal Middle Eastern Christian community. Our neighbors were Muslims and Jews. We studied together, worked together, argued together and lived together.

I grew up Christian, Arab and Israeli. I felt rooted, safe and happy. Which is why I sometimes wonder whether the Israel I keep reading about is a different country.

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

Apparently, Christians here live under siege, Christianity is being pushed out, and Jewish hostility is making Christian life increasingly impossible. It is an alarming picture, and a very strange description of the country in which I actually live.

Let me make one thing clear: There have been ugly incidents of religious radicals spitting at clergy, verbally abusing Christians and vandalizing property. Such behavior is disgraceful. Israel should confront it forcefully through law enforcement, education and religious leadership.

But then comes the question that strangely disappears from much of the discussion:

Do those extremists define Israel? Because if they do, we are going to have to rewrite our descriptions of quite a few Western democracies.

In 2025, the Anti-Defamation League recorded 6,274 antisemitic incidents in the United States, an average of 17 every day. More significantly, there were 203 physical assaults, the highest number the ADL has recorded since it began tracking such incidents.

Does that make America an antisemitic society? Of course not.

Then there is Spain.

According to Spain's Interior Ministry, hate crimes and hate incidents reached their highest recorded level in 2025, rising 23.6% in a single year. Antisemitic incidents rose 86.5% from 37 to 69 cases.

Should we therefore conclude that Spain itself is fundamentally anti-Jewish? Again, no.

ISRAEL LAUNCHES 'BIBLICAL HIGHWAY' AMID CAMPAIGN TO ERASE JEWISH HISTORY

Extremism exists in every democratic society. Sometimes it grows dangerously. Governments must confront it. But serious people understand the difference between extremists within a society and the character of the society itself.

Except, increasingly, when that society is Israel.

An extremist in Boston, Madrid or London attacks a Jew, and we correctly call him an antisemite. A fanatic spits at a Christian in Jerusalem, and suddenly we are invited to diagnose Israeli society.

That is not analysis. It is a double standard.

If you genuinely want to know whether Christians are flourishing in a country, there are better measures than the behavior of its worst citizens.

Start with the most basic question:

Are Christians disappearing?

In Israel, they are not.

DISPUTE OVER CHRISTIAN GROUPS' VISAS TO ISRAEL RESOLVED AFTER HUCKABEE THREAT

In 1950, Israel was home to roughly 34,000 Christians. Today there are about 184,000, and the community continues to grow.

Then look at what Christians actually do here.

Consider one image that tells you more about Christian integration than a hundred government brochures.

Justice Salim Joubran was an Arab Christian justice of Israel's Supreme Court. He sat on the panel that sent former Israeli president Moshe Katsav to prison. Think about that sentence. An Arab Christian judge helped send the Jewish president of the Jewish state to prison.

And nobody in Israel regarded his ethnicity or religion as an issue. He was a Supreme Court justice doing his job. That is the point.

Christians are physicians and hospital directors, academics and businesspeople, mayors, police officers, soldiers and diplomats.

I happen to be one of them.

The boy from the Christian Scouts in Jaffa eventually joined Israel's diplomatic service and became the first Christian appointed to represent Israel as an ambassador.

Today, I serve as Israel's special envoy to the Christian World, a position created specifically to deepen Israel's relationship with Christian communities around the world. Quite an elaborate way for a country supposedly hostile to Christianity to behave.

There are other inconvenient facts. In 2014, Israel formally recognized the Aramean nationality, giving members of ancient Aramaic and Syriac Christian traditions official recognition of an identity rooted in Christianity's earliest history.

Israel is also investing in Christianity's past and future here.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT

A few days ago, I visited the excavations at Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee, where archaeologists identified what is likely to have been the hometown of the Apostles Peter and Andrew.

I watched Israeli and American archaeologists, Jews and Christians, literally digging the world of Jesus back out of the earth.

There is something wonderfully inconvenient about that image: The country supposedly erasing Christianity is uncovering the village of the Apostles.

And Israel is already preparing for 2030, when Christians will mark 2,000 years since the baptism of Jesus, an anniversary expected to bring enormous numbers of pilgrims to the Holy Land.

Something interesting is happening beyond Israel's borders as well. Recent polling in Lebanon found strong support among its Christian communities for peace with Israel: 77% among Maronites and 72% among Orthodox Christians.

Perhaps Middle Eastern Christians, after watching what has happened to ancient communities in Iraq, Syria and elsewhere, are beginning to ask questions that old political slogans cannot answer.

Perhaps Jews and Christians in this region have more invested in one another's survival than generations of conflict allowed either side to admit.

None of this excuses a single act of anti-Christian hatred. A Jew who spits at a priest because he is Christian should be ashamed of himself, and Israel should make sure the law deals with him. Full stop.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Israel has work to do. Enforcement must be stronger. Religious leaders must be louder. Education must be better. I am working inside government on precisely these issues.

But I refuse to give the extremist a promotion. He is an extremist. He does not get promoted to spokesman for ten million Israelis simply because that makes for a more dramatic story.

And yet that is effectively what some of the current coverage does.

The extremist is representative, while the Christian Supreme Court justice is an exception.

The spitting teenager is Israeli, while the Christian ambassador somehow is not.

How convenient. This works because a distorted picture does not require invented facts. It requires only a carefully chosen frame. Photograph one crack in a cathedral closely enough, and you can make the entire building appear to be collapsing. The crack is real. The picture is false.

There is a broader reason this matters.

Christianity was born in this region. Yet across much of the Middle East, ancient Christian communities have suffered war, persecution, political instability, emigration and demographic decline.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Before Syria's civil war, Christians numbered over two million, and today only a few hundred thousand are estimated to remain. Iraq's Christian community has fallen from more than 1.5 million before 2003 to fewer than 200,000.

So the important Christian question of our age is not whether Israel contains unpleasant extremists. Of course it does. So do America, Spain and every other country.

The important question is:

Where in the Middle East will Christians still be living, worshiping, raising children and building a future fifty years from now?

I want the answer to include not only Jaffa, Jerusalem, Nazareth and the Galilee, but also Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Egypt and everywhere else Christians have belonged for centuries.

A few days ago at Bethsaida, standing where Peter and Andrew once lived, I was reminded that Christianity's story began here. Two thousand years later, Christians are still here. Not as archaeological artifacts or pilgrims, and certainly not merely as victims.

We worship. We raise families. We criticize our government. We build schools and careers. We serve our country and shape its future.

Israel has extremists. They deserve condemnation and prosecution. What they do not deserve is a promotion. They do not get to define Israel. And those who are so eager to let them should ask themselves why.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham, Caitlin Clark respond to Fever coach Stephanie White's pregame rant
item.description: Caitlin Clark said she felt "sick" when fans booed Stephanie White before the Indiana Fever's 106-92 win over the New York Liberty on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham addressed a viral pre-game rant by their head coach after the Indiana Fever's 106-92 win over the New York Liberty on Tuesday.

Fever coach Stephanie White dedicated her entire pre-game media availability to delivering a rant in defense of herself after she faced criticism for her response on Saturday to an incident when Chicago Sky player DiJonai Carrington smacked Cunningham in the face.

White initially told reporters Saturday that she didn't believe the hit was intentional, before declaring Tuesday that after watching footage, she believed the hit was "egregious."

Cunningham showed support for White after Tuesday's win.

FEVER SHUT DOWN SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM QUESTIONS, ABRUPTLY END PRESS CONFERENCE

"There's just been a lot of outside noise," Cunningham said. "But our locker room is good."

"Our locker room in there, it's tight, and we have each other's backs," she said. "Coach loves us."

Cunningham even defended White's first comments about the foul. White had praised Carrington's competitive nature after the game while agreeing with the officials' decision to eject her. Cunningham said White lacked a full view of the play when she spoke.

"She didn't see the clip," Cunningham said. "At the end of the day, she didn't see the clip."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

White said Tuesday of the hit, "I didn't see the play in real time. I went straight to a press conference. I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie's okay. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

Cunningham noted that White coached Carrington for two seasons with the Connecticut Sun. She said White could recognize Carrington's ability and still support her own player. Cunningham did not view White's comments as a betrayal.

"She is a hell of a player. She's a great defender," Cunningham said of Carrington. "Give her her flowers, and she didn't see it. And that's OK."

Cunningham then removed any doubt about her relationship with White.

"Me and Steph are great," she said. "Steph is great with all of us."

WHY YOU SHOULD BACK THE INDIANA FEVER TO COVER THE SPREAD AGAINST THE NEW YORK LIBERTY TUESDAY

Cunningham then shifted attention back to basketball. She said she no longer worried about the outside reaction.

"I really don't care anymore," Cunningham said. "I'm trying to keep the main thing the main thing."

Cunningham said the Fever shared the ball, defended well and found their joy again.

"With everything going on, that's kind of been hard to do," Cunningham said. "Tonight was the night that we all just, like, clicked, and we had fun, and we did it for Steph, and we did it for everyone in the locker room."

Clark offered a more personal defense. She spoke with White earlier that day and understood the toll of constant criticism.

"I think we forget a lot of times, like, we're human and she has feelings," Clark said. "There's moments that are really hard."

Clark drew from her own experience under intense scrutiny. She told White that even thick skin has limits.

"I've been through the same thing," Clark said. "There's been days where I've been really upset, and you can have the thickest skin in the world, but sometimes it does get to you."

Clark also criticized the broader climate around the team and the league. She said too many people look for conflict instead of celebrating success.

"Our world is just like, we love to hate. We love to divide," Clark said. "Nobody wants to see each other succeed."

Clark called that painful to watch. She said, "We need to do a better job at uplifting each other."

Clark said that she told White that the Fever would deliver a win for her on Tuesday.

FEVER COACH UNLOADS ON WNBA OVER TREATMENT OF CAITLIN CLARK, BUT IT'S TIME FOR CLARK TO START PUNCHING BACK

"I can assure you there was no way we were losing this game tonight," Clark said. "And I told her that before the game. Like, there was no way we were losing this game for her."

Clark also addressed the boos White heard during pregame introductions. She accepted that fans can criticize a coach but found the reaction difficult to hear.

"I hated that our fans booed her before the game," Clark said. "That made me a little sick, to be honest."

Clark said disagreement would not change the players' loyalty. She called White their head coach and said the Fever would protect the unity they had built.

"We're going to ride for her, and we're always going to have her back," Clark said. "That's never going to tear our locker room apart."

She closed by expressing affection for White and pride in the Fever's response. Clark said the team played with energy, shared the ball and competed with smiles on their faces.

"I just love her, and I feel for her because I know it can be a lot at times," Clark said. "We really just did it for her, and we did it for each other and the girls in our locker room."

White's pregame rant on Tuesday also made reference to "hate" and "divisive" forces, without referencing anyone directly, that are apparently trying to "hijack" the league.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said.

"Every day, these women put their a** on the line. Every day. When they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win. Humility will win and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

The WNBA has been at the center of a national controversy for months now, with the Fever being a recurring constant in that controversy. It started when Phoenix Mercury player Alyssa Thomas punched Clark in the throat. It escalated when Cunningham's stance on protecting women's sports was revealed and prompted a national debate on the issue with White and other coaches being mocked for their answers on the issue.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

It boiled over on Saturday after Carrington struck Cunningham and then wrote "White privilege" on Threads right after being ejected.

Now, White will try to lead the Fever through that controversy all the way to the playoffs, as the Fever are one of the hottest teams in the league and are in the driver's seat to clinch the top seed in the East.

item.title: Mike Vrabel is finally asked about his family counseling sessions made necessary by the Dianna Russini scandal
item.description: Mike Vrabel deflected a question about his family counseling sessions by pivoting to talk of offensive line combination blocks during New England Patriots camp.
item.content:encoded:
It took weeks since the New England Patriots opened their 2026 training camp and NFL rules put coach Mike Vrabel in front of reporters on a regular basis, but the question finally came on Tuesday.

Someone asked Vrabel what he learned from his counseling sessions that he previously said he was seeking after the scandal involving him and NFL reporter Dianna Russini became public.

Vrabel had announced in April he was following up difficult conversations with his family with that counseling because the photos of him and Russini hugging and holding hands and enjoying time together at a pool and spa doubtless caused friction at home.

PATRIOTS COACH MIKE VRABEL BREAKS SILENCE ON DIANNA RUSSINI PHOTOS THAT LED TO 'DIFFICULT CONVERSATIONS'

Vrabel even missed one day of the NFL Draft as part of that counseling regimen.

But then, well, radio silence.

Vrabel didn't discuss it. And he was not asked about it by the New England media. Even on the first day of camp when Vrabel faced reporters for the first time in 2026, the subject never came up.

But it did on Tuesday.

MIKE VRABEL UNTOUCHED BY DIANNA RUSSINI SCANDAL AT FIRST PRESS CONFERENCE OF PATRIOTS TRAINING CAMP

Finally.

QUESTION: "You said this offseason that you were seeking counseling. I wanted to follow up on that and see what you learned from that counseling, and how did you balance that personal commitment with getting ready for this season?"

Good work here. Journalism!

Vrabel then opened up and explained how the sessions affected his family relationships.

No he didn't.

VRABEL: "I think we always look at improvement. As we talk about getting ready for the next season, we always look at improvement and ways that we can improve individually and how we can improve as a team. It’s really critical that we continue to do that on and off the field.

"I believe in that. I believe in everything that we can do to help this football team, to help our coaches, to help myself and everybody else included.

"This journey that we are going to go on is going to be completely different than the one we went on last year. That’s all of our jobs, is to prepare for it now. So, really focused on our improvement individually and as a team, and that’s something that we can do today.

"You look at the O-line, and we talk about them and their ability to play together as a unit. There are so many combination blocks that they are involved in, and we have to be better. Again, five O-linemen have to be able to sustain a line of scrimmage, and I just walked into that meeting room and said, "How do we improve? How do we improve our combination blocks?

"We are not asking you to block everybody 1-on-1. So, I think we all have areas that we can improve on, and that includes the coaches."

That's a lot of words. But it's not anything close to insightful. Or personal.

The question about Vrabel's family counseling sessions that followed an embarrassing unfurling of a years-long relationship between him and a reporter was met with an answer that ultimately discussed offensive line combination blocks.

This doesn't make Vrabel a bad guy.

Or a bad coach.

That time he spent with the woman not his wife might, but not this. This makes him excellent at coachspeak. And expert in the art of deflection.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

It's understandable because Vrabel is wise to give an answer that does not lead to a follow-up question on an uncomfortable subject. He doesn't want to dredge up any new stories that might cause his team even the slightest distraction.

He wants a story that went viral in the spring to die this summer.

One more thing: He probably doesn't feel like he owes anyone an actual answer.

And he's correct. It's a personal matter for him and he has a right to keep it locked up.

But the question needed to be asked.

Finally, score one for journalism.

item.title: WNBA media turns Stephanie White's rehearsed rant into an 'important' attack on league critics
item.description: Stephanie White's prepared pregame rant about hate and divisiveness hijacking the WNBA drew immediate praise from ESPN analysts and reporters alike.
item.content:encoded:
Fever head coach Stephanie White opened her pregame press conference Tuesday night before Indiana’s game against the New York Liberty by reading a lengthy prepared statement about the "hate," "fear mongering" and "divisiveness" that she believes is trying to "hijack" the WNBA.

The statement included profanity, White literally banging on the table in front of her and even ended with what appeared to be a staged walk out of the press conference room without taking any questions.

That's why the reaction from the WNBA's media cheerleaders was so fascinating.

Within minutes, reporters and outlets began describing White's remarks as "passionate," "important," "impassioned" and "scathing." ESPN took the framing even further, with analysts praising White's vulnerability, honesty and commitment to love while suggesting that some of the people criticizing her are "fueled by hatred."

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

And we're just getting started.

White was heavily criticized for her reaction to DiJonai Carrington's hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham during Indiana's game against Chicago on Saturday. It seemed, to many, that White spent more energy defending an opponent who had committed a flagrant foul against her player than her own player who was left with a bloody mouth.

White explained Tuesday that she didn't see the play in real time and went directly to her postgame press conference. White said she thought the officials got the call right and said she didn't believe Carrington intentionally went for Cunningham's neck. The Fever coach said that after she watched the replay, she changed her assessment.

"Was it egregious? Absolutely," White said. "When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

It's reasonable to believe that White didn't have access to multiple replays of the play during the game and didn't see them until after she spoke to the media. Explaining that on Tuesday night made perfect sense.

But she didn't leave it there.

White said she took any suggestion that she does not have her players’ backs personally before pivoting into a broader attack on an "online community" that she accused of creating false narratives about who she is and what she represents.

"The hate, the fear mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said. "It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided."

White then borrowed Michelle Obama's famous "when they go low, we go high" line and declared that "love," "grace," "humility" and "kindness" would prevail. She followed all those calls for kindness by saying, "Everybody else can go to hell."

We could spend an entire column on the irony of that juxtaposition, but let's continue because watching the video added another layer.

White wasn't speaking extemporaneously or reacting emotionally to a question. She was clearly reading a prepared statement, repeatedly looking down at her remarks and, to my eye, trying to inject the appropriate emotion into different portions of the speech.

I didn't find her speech particularly convincing. It came across as rehearsed and performative, especially when the emotional delivery didn't seem to match the words she was reading. That's subjective, though. Anyone can watch the video and reach a different conclusion.

That's why it's borderline comical that the WNBA media ecosystem seemed to reach the exact opposite conclusion.

Underdog WNBA called White's statement "passionate." Chicago Sun-Times reporter Annie Costabile labeled it an "Important statement from Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White." ESPN's Alexa Philippou went with "impassioned," as did The Sporting News, while Meghan Hall described White's remarks as "scathing."

Individually, none of those descriptions is especially noteworthy. Taken together, though, they establish a remarkably consistent framing: White hadn't simply read a prepared statement. She had delivered something important, emotional and powerful.

JEMELE HILL IS RIGHT: WNBA FANS EXPECT JOURNALISTS TO BE 'CHEERLEADERS,' AND THAT'S NOT HOW THIS WORKS

That didn't change during ESPN's pregame coverage on "WNBA Countdown." It only became more clear that the media cheerleaders had their narrative and they were ready to roll.

Chiney Ogwumike said she saw White as someone operating under "immense pressure" and talked about how frightening it can be to show vulnerability when everyone is watching. She praised White for continuing to "speak your truth" and said the Fever coach was making an "impassioned plea" to get back to basketball and "center it around love."

That's an incredibly charitable reading of what happened. White read a prepared statement accusing unnamed people of spreading hate, fear and division, then told those people they could go to hell. ESPN turned that into a courageous display of vulnerability centered around love.

Andraya Carter then went further by questioning whether people calling for White's job had even watched enough Fever basketball to fairly judge her performance as a coach. That's a legitimate question. Social media routinely takes one clip, strips away context and turns it into a referendum on someone's entire career.

But Carter didn't stop with questioning whether the criticism was informed.

"Are you calling for her job because you watched one clip and you're piling on and you are fueled by hatred?" Carter asked.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

White had complained broadly about hate infiltrating the league without identifying the people she meant. Carter effectively filled in the blank, suggesting that at least some of White's critics weren't merely wrong, uninformed or overly emotional, but possibly "fueled by hatred."

What evidence established that? None was offered during the segment.

And, by the way, calling out White for not appropriately defending her own player during a postgame news conference is well within the bounds of normal sports criticism. Any male head coach would face the same critiques in a men's professional league were the situation comparable. Blurring legitimate criticism together with hatred and divisiveness shifts attention away from the actual issue.

Malika Andrews then praised White's "honesty and transparency," said ESPN believed it was "important" to show the statement and complimented Carter and Ogwumike for steering the network's WNBA conversations "so well and so gracefully."

Think about the progression here: a head coach makes a sweeping accusation about unnamed people spreading hatred and division on the internet. One ESPN analyst describes her as vulnerable and speaking her truth. Another wonders aloud whether the people criticizing her are actually fueled by hatred. The host then praises the coach's honesty and the panel's grace.

At no point does anyone seem especially interested in asking whether White’s central claim is actually true.

Who exactly is trying to "hijack" the WNBA? What criticism qualifies as fear mongering? Where does legitimate criticism end and harassment begin? Does disagreeing with White's handling of the Cunningham incident make someone part of the divisiveness she is condemning?

Those would seem like natural questions for people whose job is to cover the league.

Instead, ESPN did the opposite. It didn't just report White's accusation, it adopted it as the premise for its own coverage.

During the first quarter of the Fever-Liberty game, the ESPN broadcast played White's rant again.

Then reporter Holly Rowe framed the statement as a "response to the online vitriol and harassment that she and the Fever have faced" following the Chicago game. Rowe twice characterized White's remarks as "strong" and also called them "very emotional."

ESPN BURIES DIJONAI CARRINGTON DIRTY FOUL ON SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

Analyst Rebecca Lobo picked up from there.

"I've been around this league since the beginning as a former player, as a mother, as a human being," Lobo said. "My heart breaks for the players and coaches in this league right now. And the online harassment they have to deal with every day. At some point, enough is enough."

Ryan Ruocco responded, "Well said, partner," before saying everyone was looking forward to focusing more on what he called the "objectively incredible product" on the floor.

Ruocco calling the basketball "objectively" incredible is a fun rhetorical trick. Whether the quality of play is incredible is obviously a matter of opinion. Adding "objectively" doesn't make it a fact.

More importantly, ESPN had already moved past reporting White's comments and into validating the premise behind them. Remember that White vaguely referred to hate, fear mongering and divisiveness. Rowe defined the controversy for viewers as "vitriol and harassment," Lobo said her heart broke for the people dealing with it and Ruocco immediately endorsed her response.

Yes, online trolls exist. This isn't breaking news. Dealing with that can be difficult and frustrating, and I do speak from experience on that subject.

But criticism isn't automatically harassment. Calling for a coach to be fired, even if the criticism is stupid or uninformed, isn't proof that the person is trying to "hijack" a professional sports league.

If anything, it shows that the WNBA has entered normal American sports discourse, where fans criticize coaches, overreact to press conferences and call for people to be fired.

There was another theme running through all of this. White lamented that people weren't talking enough about the "great basketball" her players were playing. Ogwumike said White wanted to get back to the game everyone loves. Carter complained that "you can't just talk about basketball," while Andrews promised that the remainder of the show would focus on basketball.

Ruocco made essentially the same point during the game broadcast, saying everyone looked forward to focusing more on the product on the court.

This should sound familiar.

The WNBA and its media defenders have spent years celebrating players and coaches for speaking about subjects far beyond basketball. Politics, race, gender, social justice and culture were not treated as annoying distractions from the sport. They were presented as central features of what made the league and its players important.

Now, after White delivers a prepared speech invoking hatred, fear mongering, divisiveness, love, grace, humility and Michelle Obama, the media reaction is that everyone really wishes outsiders would stop bringing non-basketball issues into the WNBA.

Funny how that works, isn't it?

When the WNBA’s non-basketball messaging largely aligned with progressive causes, its friendly media rarely treated those conversations as an unwelcome distraction. Suddenly, though, the WNBA is in "stick to basketball" mode.

White is free to defend herself, defend her players and criticize people she believes have treated them unfairly. ESPN analysts are free to agree with her. Reporters are free to think her speech was passionate or important.

But journalists are also supposed to maintain enough distance from the people they cover to examine their claims rather than simply reinforce them.

The WNBA's friendly media ecosystem didn't merely report what Stephanie White said. It immediately validated what she said, supplied motives for the people she was attacking and elevated a rehearsed pregame rant into an "important" emotional flashpoint.

White said love, grace, humility and kindness would win.

ESPN agreed.

And everybody who doesn't buy it can apparently go to hell.

item.title: 'No better group': Veteran says special ops should get same concealed carry permit as retired cops
item.description: The Special Operations Forces Concealed Carry Act would extend Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act-style privileges to qualified special operator veterans.
item.content:encoded:
A retired Army special operations veteran is urging Congress to give qualified former special operators nationwide concealed carry privileges enjoyed by retired U.S. law enforcement officers, arguing the elite troops are uniquely trained to protect themselves and Americans.

"It needs to happen," Gavin Glasenapp, who served 20 years and 12 combat deployments in the Army, told Fox News Digital on Monday.

The Special Operations Forces Concealed Carry Act was put forward last week by Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., months after a companion bill by the same name in the House was introduced in April by Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C.

"These are proven men and women," Glasenapp, the training operations manager at Delta Defense for the U.S. Concealed Carry Association (USCCA) said, adding "They're specially selected, uniquely trained."

TRUMP’S PUSH FOR NATIONAL CONCEALED CARRY RECIPROCITY WOULD PROTECT GOOD GUYS WITH GUNS

"I can think of no better group of people to be equipped to defend themselves and others around them. In fact, that's part of our core values here at Delta Defense.

"We believe every American has the inalienable right to self-defense, and I can think of no better group that to really emulate that and really show you what that looks like."

More well-trained good guys with guns to stop the bad guys with guns will help keep America safe again, Second Amendment advocates argue.

Last month, President Donald Trump trolled his critics and gun-control advocates with a post that went viral: "Over 273 Americans have been shot since the war in Iran ... in Chicago."

CHICAGO'S DEADLY JUNETEENTH WEEKEND LEAVES 7 DEAD AS TRUMP SHAMES DEM GOV FOR INACTION

Chicago is among the Democrat-run cities with strict gun laws and, yet, a raging gun violence crisis every summer.

Notably, an armed bystander last week in Idaho, strapped by the shoulder with an FN Five-seveN semi-automatic pistol, was able to engage a mass shooter, forcing him to flee and saving countless lives, local police hailed. That bystander, Jordan Salinas, had concealed carry training, and local police noted he followed "observe, orient, decide and act" (OODA) protocol as a good guy with a gun able to help stop a bad guy with one.

"That would be the OODA loop," Glasenapp said.

"That's kind of become almost a university taught system of being situationally aware. You know, observing a threat and making decisions as far as what your next steps are going to be. And the big thing with that OODA loop is it's just that: It's a loop. You should constantly be observing, orienting on things, deciding, acting, and then redoing it over and over again."

MARYLAND SYNAGOGUE SUES COUNTY OVER LAW RESTRICTING CONCEALED CARRY NEAR HOUSES OF WORSHIP

Nationwide concealed carry reciprocity, making it lawfully easier to carry concealed state to state, has faced congressional obstruction from gun-control advocates, but expanding the Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act (LEOSA) to special ops veterans would allow more good guys with guns to stop bad guys with guns.

It also could be a baby step, ultimately, in gun-rights advocates' push for nationwide reciprocity.

The fact highly trained special operations veterans are not afforded the permission to carry concealed firearms across state lines might be a surprise to some.

"[LEOSA] allows retired law enforcement officers to carry concealed throughout the country, which is very convenient, actually, because sometimes state laws as far as concealed carry or possessing weapons can be very different when you travel state to state," Glasenapp said.

"So, for example, if you're a retired law officer, and you're on a cross-country road trip with your family, that definitely streamlines things a lot. You're not having to check things like a reciprocity app."

COMBAT VET SENATOR CHOKES UP OVER FALLEN FRIEND IN FIERY FLOOR SPEECH ABOUT IRAN WAR: ‘WE WILL FINISH IT’

The most popular reciprocity app is the USCCA Concealed Carry app, which provides a live interactive permit reciprocity map, state gun laws, and permit management tools for all 50 states.

READ THE BILL – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

A key distinction between the proposed Sheehy Senate bill and Harrigan's House version is annual certification requirements for special ops veterans.

"Our Special Operations Forces spend their careers protecting the American people with unmatched discipline, judgment, and professionalism," Sheehy wrote in a statement.

"This bill honors that reality by giving qualified special operators the same nationwide concealed carry privileges already afforded to retired law enforcement officers. Our elite warfighters never stop serving, and this bill ensures the law reflects the trust they’ve earned through a lifetime of sacrifice."

Sheehy's version requires a yearly, state-standard, active-duty-level firearms qualification at the individual’s expense, plus completion of a Justice Department-certified "Concealed Carry Use of Force in Society" course before carrying.

SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN BLUE STATE'S 'VAMPIRE RULE' IN MAJOR WIN FOR GUN RIGHTS

Harrigan's bill just expands the LEOSA standards to special ops veterans and calls for "no separate certification of firearms training is required for a qualified special operator."

"I don't believe the annual re-certification requirement should be required for either the proposed special operations forces concealed carry act or the current HR 218/LEOSA," according to Glasenapp, who urges regular training regardless if it is required. 

"Both of these communities have spent their professional careers training and qualifying with various handguns and other small arms."

The Senate bill defines a qualified special operator as a former member of the armed forces who went through a special operations assessment, was selected for qualification training and held a special warfare or special operations occupational specialty or skill designator recognized by U.S. Special Operations Command.

Glasenapp said the distinction matters because firearms proficiency is a fundamental and continually reinforced part of training for many of the operators the legislation is intended to cover.

An infantryman or infantry officer in the Army’s 75th Ranger Regiment, for example, would be "intimately familiar with small arms," including rifles and handguns, he said.

"There’s going to be continuing training on that," Glasenapp said, noting that firearms skills can deteriorate without practice.

Special operators have another advantage when it comes to navigating different rules: years of operating under changing restrictions in different jurisdictions and even different countries.

"These are folks that have not only dealt with changing state lines, but different rules and different regulations in different countries," Glasenapp said. "We’re talking international travel and dealing with rules of engagement that are constantly changing depending on what theater you’re in.

"They can definitely adapt on the fly."

READ THE HOUSE VERSION OF THE BILL – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

Glasenapp also rejected the notion that military experience alone means special operations veterans would treat civilian concealed carry like operating in a combat zone – a fear gun-control advocates have.

He said he held a Tennessee concealed carry permit himself while serving on active duty and stressed that carrying a firearm as a civilian comes with different legal responsibilities.

"What you’re doing as a civilian carrying every day … is going to be different than when you’re in a combat zone," said Glasenapp, who said he deployed 12 times during his military career.

"Get familiar with local, state and federal law as far as what you can and can’t do," he said. "You’ve got to make different decisions and act in different ways."

The veteran also said he would support broader nationwide concealed carry reciprocity, arguing that gun owners currently face a complicated patchwork of laws when traveling between states.

But, on the narrower proposal before Congress, Glasenapp said he believes special operators have already demonstrated the judgment and skills necessary to earn the expanded protection.

"I certainly hope this passes and becomes U.S. code," Glasenapp said.

"I think it needs to happen."

item.title: WATCH: Neighbor’s double take helped police identify accused wildfire arsonist as flames raced nearby
item.description: Paul Child spotted a stranger near railroad tracks twice before smoke rose, leading to a field showup that helped police ID accused arsonist Farinacci.
item.content:encoded:
Paul Child drove past a stranger twice near railroad tracks outside his Washington home, then watched smoke rise about 10 minutes after the man crouched in nearby bushes – setting off a chain of events that helped police identify an accused wildfire arsonist.

Newly obtained bodycam footage shows officers evacuating Child’s family and taking him, his grandson and the boy’s friend to a field showup after detaining a man who matched their description.

While Child and the other witnesses waited near the showup scene, bodycam footage captured an officer saying the detained man had "a whole fanny pack full of matches."

The video does not show the alleged matches or establish how they were recovered.

MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE

Child said he and the other witnesses — his grandson and his grandson’s friend — were not told about the alleged matches or other items before they were asked to view the detained man.

"We thought he had a backpack," Child told Fox News Digital. "They didn’t say anything to us anyway about the fanny pack with matches, cigarettes [and] I guess lighter in it."

CANADIAN WILDFIRE SMOKE IGNITES CROSS-BORDER FEUD OVER OTTAWA'S 'WILLFUL NEGLIGENCE'

Child told Fox News Digital that he, his grandson and the grandson’s friend spotted a man twice near railroad tracks close to the apparent fire origin. The second time, Child said, the man’s behavior appeared unusual.

"He was kind of bent over and looked like he was doing something in the bushes," Child said. "He got up, saw us. When he saw us, he turned to face us and kind of was pacing back and forth nervously."

Child said there was no smoke when the group last saw the man. Within about 10 minutes of returning home, however, he said smoke began rising about a half-mile away.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Bodycam footage from the Airway Heights Police Department shows smoke billowing in the distance as Officer Pace speaks with Child’s family about evacuating. The officer later tells them police may have detained "your guy" and that they could be asked to take part in a showup.

A field showup is an in-person identification procedure in which witnesses view a person detained shortly after an incident.

While the footage does not show the identification, Child said Pace escorted him and the two boys to a location about a mile and a half from his home.

"We pulled off to the side of the road, and they got an individual out from the back of the … Spokane County deputy car," Child said. "We looked at him, and all three of us gave them [a] positive, 100% positive ID that’s who we’d seen in the area just before the fire started."

Child said he and the two teen witnesses positively identified the detained man during the field showup. Authorities later identified the man as Aaron Forrest Farinacci.

SPOKANE FIRE SURVIVOR FINDS 'JOY' THROUGH JESUS AFTER ALLEGED ARSON DESTROYS HOME AND BELONGINGS

The Aug. 1 field showup did not immediately lead to charges. Farinacci was released after witnesses identified the detained man, then was arrested on charges two days later, on Aug. 3.

Child said he did not initially realize Farinacci had been released.

"I was like, well, thank God, because … I thought they had him detained the whole time. I didn’t realize they didn’t have probable cause to hold him for a couple days. … He could walk right back up that road," Child said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails Fire, one of three blazes that have burned across Spokane and Stevens counties since Aug. 1. The Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane fires had burned a combined 10,002 acres and damaged or destroyed more than 920 structures, Spokane fire officials reported Monday.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Farinacci, who was initially held on $1 million bail, appeared in court Thursday, when a judge doubled his bail to $2 million. He also faces four additional arson charges after court documents alleged he admitted to setting 25 fires in the area since 2025.

Court documents reviewed by Fox News Digital allege Farinacci monitored weather apps to identify ideal fire conditions and built a delayed ignition device to start the Old Trails Fire.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Although Farinacci initially denied involvement in the Old Trails Fire during questioning after his Aug. 3 arrest, court documents allege he later confessed to planning and setting the blaze. The documents say he planned the fire for two weeks.

Investigators allege Farinacci built a time-delay device from paper, matches, cigarettes and rubber bands modeled after one used by serial arsonist John Leonard Orr. Court documents also allege he deliberately set simultaneous fires at other times to distract and thin out emergency response crews.

SEND US A TIP

As the wildfire spread, Child’s family gathered pets and belongings before evacuating their home.

"It was pretty chaotic," Child said. "I forgot my medications. We forgot leashes for the dogs or dog food and all that stuff."

GOT A TIP?

Child said the flames came no closer than about a quarter-mile from his home, but he feared a shift in the wind could have sent the fast-moving fire toward his property within minutes.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Looking back, Child said he sees his decision to alert police as only one part of the response.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"I’m sorry I wasn’t able to stop him from doing what he did," Child said, adding that he believes he played only a small part in the man being caught. "It was kind of like, well, good. At least he’s off the street."

"I mean, he wasn’t going to stop," Child added. "Fortunately, he didn’t kill anybody this time, but I imagine his luck on that was going to run out if he continued to set fires."

Fox News Digital’s Emma Bussey contributed to this report.

item.title: Meghan Markle’s royal exit had warning signs years earlier, veteran correspondent reveals
item.description: Simon Vigar's new book details how Meghan Markle's 2018 royal tour of Australia exposed the first cracks in her relationship with palace staff.
item.content:encoded:
Meghan Markle’s rocky tenure as a working royal may have stemmed from a "culture clash" with palace aides, according to a veteran royal correspondent who covered her time as a working royal.

Simon Vigar, one of Britain's longest-serving royal correspondents, examines those tensions in his new book, "The Four Wives of Windsor."

Kensington Palace told Fox News Digital it does not comment on books. A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex told Fox News Digital, "This is not something we would comment on."

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

"There was a culture clash there," Vigar told Fox News Digital. "I think it's a crying shame. It was avoidable, and egos got in the way on both sides. I think she thought that there would be more control over events, public events, than there was. ... The narrative now is that the British media was always against Harry and Meghan. That is not how I remember it, and many of my colleagues remember it."

"Harry and Meghan were great," Vigar said. "I saw her on her first engagement in Nottingham. She was brilliant with the crowds. She was an absolute natural, which is why it's so sad that they're not part of [the working royals] now. The tour of Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and Tonga [in 2018] went really well.

"The crowds were massive. But ... the palace press officers were trying to spin three different stories after that. One person was in tears from the Kensington Palace team because of how it had all gone pear-shaped, as we say in the U.K."

WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE FACED ROYAL FAMILY ‘CULTURE CLASH’: AUTHOR

Meghan, a former American actress who starred in the legal drama "Suits," became the Duchess of Sussex when she married Prince Harry in 2018. The palace announced Meghan's pregnancy shortly after the couple arrived in Sydney for their royal tour that October.

Vigar covered the royal tour and wrote that it exposed some of the first significant cracks in Meghan's role as a working royal. According to Vigar, Meghan was accustomed to a public life where "everything was micromanaged in a far more controlled environment."

"Those levels of Hollywood control-freakery, as courtiers say, are incompatible with the public service role of the monarchy," he wrote. Vigar also quoted an anonymous senior staffer as saying, "My overall sense is Meghan realized it was hard work and not that glamorous. It's not about you."

Vigar wrote that during the royal tour, Meghan was scheduled to visit Suva Market in Fiji for an engagement highlighting women's economic empowerment. She planned to meet with vendors connected to the cause, but the visit ended earlier than planned.

"There were all these people queuing up to meet her," Vigar recalled. "... In the first few minutes, it all ended very quickly. Team Sussex said it was a security issue. That is denied by other people."

Reports at the time attributed the shortened visit to security concerns as crowds gathered to see Meghan.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"... If it was a security issue, the Scotland Yard bodyguards would never have allowed her to arrive. They have an advanced team there. They have a team with her. They wouldn't have let her get out of the car if they thought it was a big security issue."

"Was it because it was too chaotic or too hot? Well, it wasn't chaotic really," Vigar said. "It was a very well-planned route through the market. It may have been illness, although that's not what Team Sussex said. In which case, why come down in the first place? And she looked OK. [But] there was a moment in the market where she looked at one of her assistants and the whole mood changed. It all went fast-forward. And my cameraman was being pushed out of the way."

"The women I was with had been waiting for ages to see her," Vigar continued. "One of them had handmade raffia fans with Harry and Meghan in them. She didn't get to meet her. She just zoomed past her, and that was that. Meghan was off. It was very strange. ... And I suppose that was an early sign in retrospect. That was an early sign that there was a mismatch in expectations."

Vigar noted that the Duchess of Sussex was working on "an intense schedule" while pregnant during the overseas tour.

"Meghan understood ‘the show’ bit but not the cultural side of the royal family," one senior aide told Vigar.

Valentine Low, then royal correspondent for The Times of London, reported in 2021 that Jason Knauf, who had served as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s communications secretary, had submitted a bullying complaint concerning Meghan in 2018. The Sussexes’ lawyers rebutted the allegations, while a spokesperson for the couple said the duchess was "saddened by this latest attack on her character."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Vigar argued that Meghan didn't just marry a prince. She also entered an institution with its own rules, rhythms and intense press scrutiny — a sharp contrast with Hollywood, where, he said, publicists can exert far more control over appearances, interviews and publicity.

"The press team at Kensington Palace is pretty small, let's say, compared to a movie premiere in Hollywood or a movie premiere in London," he explained. "It's a tiny press team, and they're involved in this institution, this royal family, which is on the front pages almost every single day. They have to roll with it. They have to roll with events, and they have to try and shape them in the best way they can."

"Harry understood it," Vigar argued. "Meghan, by her own admission, didn't know much about the British royal family or who some of them were. It was just a different level of expectation. Whereas Catherine, Camilla, Lady Diana Spencer, who was an aristocrat and the most aristocratic of all four of them, they just understood the British family even more. I think the problem was it was a culture clash. It's an American lady marrying into the most upper-class British family possible."

A royal aide told Vigar that working royals are expected to fulfill public engagements even when they do not feel their best: "Even if they are feeling grotty, they turn up and they do the job."

In the book, Vigar wrote that there is nothing "showbiz" about "cold palaces and a life of smiling, waving and turning up."

According to reports, several palace employees left their positions while working for Harry and Meghan. Former aides later made allegations about Meghan's treatment of staff, including claims that her behavior contributed to some employees leaving. Meghan has strongly denied allegations that she bullied palace staff.

"The idea that the Kensington Palace press team was briefing against Meghan from day one, I just don't agree with," Vigar told Fox News Digital. "That's obviously what Harry and Meghan believe, but I know, and my colleagues know that actually, the reverse is true. People were working very hard to support her. And unfortunately, it didn't work out, and it went downhill … By the end of 2019, they both wanted out."

WATCH: PRINCE HARRY BELIEVED ROYAL FAMILY COULD HAVE ALLOWED A HYBRID ROLE: AUTHOR

Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and later moved to California, where they live with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The couple have repeatedly criticized the British tabloid press and said they did not receive adequate support from the royal institution.

item.title: Wine expert says one common habit could be sabotaging every sip
item.description: A sommelier says sipping water before tasting wine can alter your palate instead of cleansing it. Patience, not hydration, she says, is the key to experiencing a wine's true flavors.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to experience a wine's full range of flavors, sipping water before or between tastes may seem like a natural way to cleanse your palate — but a sommelier says it could keep you from tasting the wine as intended.

"Anything you take in your mouth before your first sip of wine is going to alter its true colors," New York-based sommelier and wine educator Sarah Looper told Fox News Digital.

To judge a wine accurately, Looper recommends giving it a few tastes. The first sip of wine "sets the tone," she said. It's at this point that you should also smell the wine.

DINERS DITCHING BOTTLES OF WINE FOR THE TABLE AS HEALTHY LIVING AND RISING COSTS RESHAPE RESTAURANT HABITS

"Because we smell better with our mouths, if we put those aromatic molecules on our mouth first, we'll actually smell the wine better when it comes to our second sip, because you're adapting your palate to what the wine really is," she said.

Looper is describing a process called retronasal olfaction, which happens when aromas from food or drink travel from the mouth to the nose, affecting how we perceive flavor.

People's palates also vary, Looper said, pointing to differences in factors such as oral pH and taste sensitivity.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"What you put on your palate, whether it's a sugary and highly acidic and effervescent Coca-Cola, or a sip of something like an Old-Fashioned that's really alcoholic and really sweet and woody, that will totally jack your palate," she said. 

"You can't go from something like that and then move into your wine and expect your brain and your palate to be able to evaluate it."

The key to resetting your palate isn't water, but patience, Looper said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"You have to give yourself a little bit of time and then take a first sip of that wine, adapt your brain to what you're tasting and then take a second sip," she said. 

"And it's that second sip, and even that third sip, that will really set the wine in your brain and on your mouth for what it's supposed to be."

The flavors in wine also evolve after it is poured and interacts with oxygen, Food & Wine reported, so wine may taste different several minutes after the initial sip.

On days when she's tasting wine in a professional capacity, Looper has a ritual she said is comparable to a professional athlete preparing for game day.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"I will brush my teeth, but early, but then I will have a black coffee early to reset my palate," she said. "Then I don't put anything else on my palate except sips of water on my way to the venue."

Looper’s advice doesn’t mean wine drinkers should avoid staying hydrated, of course. Rather, she said she prefers to give her palate time to settle before evaluating a wine instead of relying on water immediately beforehand to "reset" it.

It’s easy to get caught up in the so-called rules of tasting wine and pairing it, Looper said. A simple way to make the most of the experience is to smell the wine first, take a small sip, let it coat your palate, and then pause before taking a second sip to notice how the aromas and flavors develop, she said.

"It's not so much about right or wrong," she said. "It's about, what do you like? What do you enjoy? What tastes good to you? Take those rules, bend them a little bit and see if an alternative [pairing] works. Maybe you'll love it."

item.title: Ex-New Jersey mayor, her husband charged for using fake ballot signatures after she pleaded guilty to DUI
item.description: Gina LaPlaca and her husband Jason Carty face ballot fraud charges after allegedly using fake signatures on her Democratic primary petition in New Jersey.
item.content:encoded:
A former New Jersey mayor who previously pleaded guilty in a DUI case involving her child is facing new charges alongside her husband after prosecutors alleged false signatures appeared on her nominating petition for a Democratic primary race.

Gina LaPlaca, the former mayor of Lumberton Township who remains a member of the township committee, was charged with making a false statement under oath, knowingly filing a false petition, tampering with public records and falsifying or tampering with records, the Burlington County Prosecutor's Office announced Tuesday.

LaPlaca's husband, Jason Carty, was also charged with knowingly filing a false petition, tampering with public records and falsifying or tampering with records.

The petition submitted by Carty to the Lumberton Township Municipal Clerk for the primary election included an affidavit signed by LaPlaca saying she "personally circulated the petition [and] that such petition was signed by each of the signers thereof in his/her own handwriting."

DEM OFFICIAL PLEADS GUILTY TO CHILD ABUSE FOR DRIVING DRUNK AT TRIPLE LEGAL LIMIT, ENTERS DIVERSION PROGRAM

An investigation found that LaPlaca, 47, and Carty, 49, had collected signatures for the petition, prosecutors said. 

"An investigation by the Prosecutor’s Office revealed that multiple individuals whose names and purported signatures appeared on LaPlaca's nominating petition indicated they had neither signed the petition nor authorized anyone to do so on their behalf in support of the candidate's nomination," the Burlington County Prosecutor's Office said.

Prosecutors said that without the allegedly fraudulent signatures, LaPlaca's petition would not have contained enough valid signatures to qualify her as a candidate for the June 2026 Democratic primary for Lumberton Township Committee.

VIRGINIA SCHOOL SAFETY DIRECTOR CHARGED WITH DUI AFTER WINTER STORM

LaPlaca and Carty have a court appearance scheduled on Sept. 21 in Mount Holly, New Jersey.

LaPlaca served as Lumberton's mayor from 2021 to 2025. Although she left the mayor's post, she retained her seat on the township committee, with her current term set to expire at the end of this year.

She sought re-election to the committee in the June Democratic primary but finished third in the contest for two open seats, behind Mayor Terrance Benson and his running mate, Kendra Hatfield.

The new allegations come after LaPlaca pleaded guilty earlier this year in a DUI case stemming from an incident in which her child was in the vehicle.

Prosecutors said LaPlaca was intoxicated when she picked up her child from daycare in March 2025. Witness video showed her vehicle swerving out of its lane and nearly striking a utility pole while the child was inside.

Police said her blood alcohol concentration was 0.30%, more than three times the legal limit of 0.08%.

LaPlaca was sentenced to three years of supervision under a pretrial intervention program, including mandatory attendance at Alcoholics Anonymous meetings.

item.title: REP BRIAN MAST: I want unsafe truckers off our highways — and America's veterans in their seats
item.description: Freedom Haulers fast-tracks veterans into trucking while removing foreign drivers who fail English and skills tests on U.S. roads.
item.content:encoded:
One year ago this week, three Floridians senselessly lost their lives on Florida’s Turnpike near Fort Pierce due to the complete and utter recklessness of a truck driver with an illegal CDL license. If you are a foreign national driving a commercial truck in America, you should have to meet the same basic safety requirements as everyone else. 

Three people died for doing nothing more than simply driving down the highway when a tractor-trailer driver made an illegal U-turn through an access point, cutting across traffic and leaving an approaching minivan with nowhere to go.

Their families will carry that loss for the rest of their lives.

ILLEGAL ALIEN FAILED CDL TEST 10 TIMES IN 2 MONTHS BEFORE FATAL FLORIDA CRASH THAT KILLED 3

We cannot bring those Americans back. But we can decide who drives on our highways and whether their senseless deaths are going to be another tragedy we forget — or a warning that finally forces us to fix a broken system.

I choose the latter.

America should not lower our standards to accommodate foreign nationals who cannot meet basic commercial-driving requirements. Full stop. Shortsighted state policies and lax federal oversight, like California issuing Non-Domiciled CDLs without rigorous verification of legal work status or language skills, are endangering each and every American citizen.

And this doesn’t have to be the case. We have the best trained drivers in the world. American veterans already possess the discipline, training, and experience needed on the road, and I can’t think of better training for our commercial trucking industry.

SEC SEAN DUFFY: FREEDOM HAULERS PUTS VETERANS IN THE DRIVERS' SEATS OF NEW CAREERS

That is what President Trump’s Freedom Haulers initiative is about, and that’s why I’m proud to introduce the bill to make it law.

Freedom Haulers recognizes something the rest of the country should have recognized long ago: military experience counts. Veterans have the discipline, precision, accountability and experience that trucking demands. Qualified veterans with military heavy-vehicle experience can use existing federal waivers to avoid redundant road testing and get into the industry faster.

Now Congress needs to make that policy permanent.

That is why I am introducing new Freedom Haulers legislation to codify the program.

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

It is about getting Americans who served this country into the trucking industry while getting dangerous, unqualified foreign drivers off our roads. The Trump administration has made clear that Freedom Haulers is part of a broader effort to crack down on dangerous foreign drivers, restore integrity to the trucking industry, and give our veterans good-paying jobs here at home.

That’s why, with my bill and President Trump’s initiative, we will be creating a program that fast-tracks American veterans into the trucking industry, allowing veterans with qualifying military driving experience to skip the CDL knowledge test, in addition to existing mechanisms that can let them bypass the road/skills test, and use veterans’ benefits to pay for CDL training.

Federal law already requires commercial drivers to speak English and read road signs, but lax enforcement has allowed drivers who scored as low as 2 out of 12 on proficiency tests onto our highways.

VIRGINIA BUS CRASH THAT KILLED FIVE INVOLVED DRIVER WHO DOESN'T SPEAK ENGLISH, SEAN DUFFY SAYS

Foreign nationals driving on our roads, who failed English proficiency tests, who can’t understand our road signs, and who don’t know the driving laws are a real problem in our country, and we don’t need to lose another American because of it.

It ends now.

We need to get unqualified and unauthorized foreign drivers off the road — and put American veterans behind the wheel.

If you are driving a commercial truck on American highways — regardless of where you were born — you must meet strict, non-negotiable safety requirements.

If you are a foreign national driving a commercial truck in America, you should have to meet the same basic safety requirements as everyone else.

TRUMP ADMIN TRUCKING CRACKDOWN LANDS 51 IMMIGRATION DETENTIONS, 36 ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY VIOLATIONS

If you cannot demonstrate English proficiency, you should not be behind the wheel of an 80,000-pound vehicle. If you cannot pass the required skills test, you should not have a commercial driver's license. If you are improperly licensed, improperly authorized or otherwise fail the requirements of federal law, you should be taken off the road.

This isn't complicated.

It isn't anti-immigrant.

It isn't unfair.

It's common sense.

DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR

American families should not have to share the highway with someone who cannot communicate with law enforcement or demonstrate that they can safely operate a commercial vehicle.

The tragedy in Fort Pierce, that happened just a few miles from my home, showed why that matters.

According to the facts, the driver, who entered our country illegally, had scored just 2 out of 12 on an English proficiency test but was still given a CDL license by California. He was also operating a commercial tractor-trailer despite failing to obtain a work authorization.

TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

That should never happen again.

We should not be bending the rules for people who fail them.

We should be enforcing the rules — and then giving Americans who have already proven themselves an opportunity to do the job.

That is where our veterans come in.

For years, we asked American service members to operate massive military vehicles carrying troops, fuel and equipment in some of the most dangerous environments on Earth. We trusted them with millions of dollars of equipment. We trusted them with the lives of their fellow Americans.

ARMY VET, TRUCKING EXECUTIVE RAVES OVER TRUMP PLAN TO BOLSTER BLUE COLLAR INDUSTRY BY FAST-TRACKING VETERANS

While programs exist to waive the driving test for some veterans, bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent state rules still make them jump through unnecessary hoops, including redundant written exams. We should cut that red tape completely.

We should be removing barriers for American veterans — not lowering standards for foreign drivers.

We should be recruiting the Americans who have already demonstrated that they can do the job — not importing people who cannot meet the minimum requirements to do it safely.

And we should be making one thing absolutely clear: A commercial driver's license is not a participation trophy.

It is permission to operate a machine weighing tens of thousands of pounds alongside American families.

That privilege comes with an enormous responsibility.

If you fail the English test, you're off the road.

If you fail the skills test, you're off the road.

If your license was improperly issued, you're off the road.

If you are not legally authorized to hold the credential that allows you to operate a commercial vehicle, you're off the road.

There should be no loopholes. No excuses. No second set of standards.

And when those drivers are removed, we should fill those seats with Americans who earned the right to be there.

Our veterans have already answered the call.

They've driven military trucks.

They've followed orders.

They've operated under pressure.

Now we should give them another mission: Keep America moving.

The anniversary of the Fort Pierce crash is a reminder of what happens when we continue to let dangerous people go on our roads.

We owe those three victims more than thoughts and prayers.

We owe their families action.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That means enforcing the rules against foreign nationals who cannot meet our standards. It means making sure every commercial driver can communicate in English and demonstrate the skills necessary to safely operate a big rig. And it means opening the door for American veterans who have already demonstrated those abilities.

We don't need to lower the bar.

We need to enforce it.

We don't need to look overseas for qualified drivers while qualified Americans are standing at the door.

We need to put our veterans behind the wheel.

Get unqualified foreign drivers off America's roads.

Put American veterans behind the wheel.

And make our highways safe again.
